projects.problemStatement: Manual roll-call in large lecture halls wastes 5–8 minutes per class, is easy to proxy, and produces no reliable attendance analytics for faculty.
projects.aim: Build a contactless, anti-proxy attendance system that marks attendance in under 10 seconds per student and gives faculty real-time analytics.
objectives: Achieve ≥95% recognition accuracy under normal classroom lighting
Mark a full 60-student class in under 2 minutes
Provide faculty with per-student attendance trends and defaulter alerts
Run fully offline on a Raspberry Pi edge device
projects.approach: We validated feasibility with a Haar-cascade baseline, then moved to a fine-tuned FaceNet embedding model with cosine-similarity matching. The pipeline runs on a Raspberry Pi 4 with a Pi Camera; a Flask API writes to PostgreSQL and a React dashboard consumes the REST layer. Three pilot classes with real students drove iterations on lighting thresholds and embedding distance cut-offs.
developmentChallenges: Recognition accuracy collapsed in backlit classrooms — fixed with CLAHE preprocessing and a second enrolment photo per student
Raspberry Pi thermal throttling during 60-student inference — solved with frame batching and active cooling
PostgreSQL connection pooling under concurrent Flask workers caused timeouts — moved to a single async worker with a queue
mistakes: Left dataset cleaning until week 12 — 20% of enrolment photos were unusable and had to be re-collected
Chose a heavy face model before benchmarking on the Pi, then had to rewrite the inference layer
No automated tests until the final sprint, which made refactoring terrifying
learning: Edge ML deployment is a thermal and memory problem as much as an accuracy problem
Data quality beats model size for face recognition
Writing tests early pays for itself the moment you refactor
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I went in able to train a model in a notebook and came out able to ship one on constrained hardware. The biggest shift was learning to measure before optimising — and to treat data collection as a first-class engineering task.

projects.problemStatement: Small clinics still run appointments, prescriptions and billing on paper registers, causing lost records, double-bookings and hours of manual reconciliation.
projects.aim: Deliver an affordable multi-tenant clinic management platform covering appointments, patient records, prescriptions and billing in one place.
objectives: Support multiple clinics (tenants) with isolated data
Reduce appointment booking time to under 30 seconds
Generate printable prescriptions and invoices
Work on low-end Android tablets used at reception
projects.approach: We modelled the domain first (patient → visit → prescription → invoice) with Prisma, then built a Next.js App Router front end with server components for the heavy tables. Stripe handles subscription billing for clinics; role-based access separates receptionists, doctors and admins. We tested with two real clinics during a two-week pilot.
developmentChallenges: Multi-tenancy data isolation was error-prone — solved with a tenant-scoped Prisma client wrapper
Low-end tablets choked on the original client-side data tables — moved to server-side pagination
Stripe webhook idempotency caused duplicate invoices until we added an event log table
mistakes: Designed the schema before talking to real receptionists — had to add walk-in appointments late
Used client-side rendering for everything at first, then refactored half the app to server components
Underestimated print styling; prescriptions looked broken on thermal printers
learning: Domain modelling conversations save weeks of refactoring
Server components dramatically reduce bundle size for data-heavy dashboards
Payment webhooks must be idempotent from day one
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to treat non-technical users as co-designers rather than test subjects. My biggest growth was in database design and in shipping a multi-tenant product responsibly.

projects.problemStatement: Smallholder farmers lose 20–40% of yield to diseases they cannot identify in time, and agricultural extension officers are too few to visit every farm.
projects.aim: Give farmers an offline-capable mobile tool that identifies crop diseases from a leaf photo and recommends low-cost treatments.
objectives: Classify 12 common diseases across 4 crops with ≥90% top-1 accuracy
Run inference on-device without internet
Provide treatment advice in local language
Keep the app under 40 MB
projects.approach: We collected 18k leaf images from field visits and open datasets, then trained a MobileNetV3 model with heavy augmentation. The model was quantised to TFLite and shipped inside a Flutter app; a FastAPI service serves model updates and aggregated disease heatmaps for extension officers.
developmentChallenges: Class imbalance — some diseases had 30× fewer samples; fixed with focal loss and targeted collection drives
Model drifted on real field photos vs. lab images — added field-image fine-tuning
On-device inference was slow on budget phones — solved with INT8 quantisation and input resizing
mistakes: Trained the first model on clean lab images only — accuracy dropped 25 points in the field
Shipped without a fallback for unknown diseases, so the model confidently mislabelled healthy leaves
Ignored app size until the end; had to strip several dependencies
learning: Field data is not optional for agricultural ML
Quantisation is a product decision, not just an optimisation
Always include an 'unknown' class and a confidence threshold
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned that ML products live or die on data collection pipelines. I also became much better at mobile performance work and at communicating model limitations honestly.

projects.problemStatement: Women travelling alone at night have no fast, discreet way to alert trusted contacts or authorities when they feel unsafe.
projects.aim: Build a one-tap SOS app that shares live location with trusted contacts and local authorities, and works even on a locked screen.
objectives: Trigger SOS in under 2 seconds from the lock screen
Share live location for 30 minutes after trigger
Send SMS fallback when data is unavailable
Keep battery impact under 3% per hour
projects.approach: We used Flutter for a single codebase, Firebase for auth and realtime location, and a small Node.js service to fan out SMS via Twilio. A home-screen widget and a volume-button shortcut trigger SOS without unlocking. We ran a safety review with a local NGO before launch.
developmentChallenges: Background location on iOS is heavily restricted — solved with significant-change API plus foreground service on Android
Battery drain during live tracking — batched location updates and reduced GPS accuracy after 5 minutes
SMS fallback reliability varied by carrier — added a retry queue and delivery receipts
mistakes: Assumed background location 'just works' on both platforms; lost two weeks to platform differences
Did not test on low-end devices until late — animations janked badly
No accessibility review until the end; the SOS button was hard to hit for users with motor impairments
learning: Mobile platform constraints are the real architecture
Battery and reliability are safety features, not nice-to-haves
Accessibility is a safety requirement for this kind of app
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I became far more disciplined about platform-specific behaviour and about testing on real, cheap hardware. I also learned to bring domain experts (the NGO) into the design process early.

projects.problemStatement: Commuters wait 20–40 minutes for buses with no reliable arrival information, and operators have no visibility into fleet positions.
projects.aim: Provide real-time bus locations and ETA predictions to commuters via a web app, and a fleet dashboard for operators.
objectives: Track 10 buses with ≤30 second location lag
Predict ETA within ±3 minutes
Run for 12 hours on a single charge
Handle tunnel and urban-canyon GPS dropouts
projects.approach: ESP32 boards with GPS modules publish positions over MQTT to a Node.js ingest service backed by Redis for live state and PostgreSQL for history. A React map shows live buses and ETAs computed from recent segment speeds. We deployed on five routes with two partner operators.
developmentChallenges: GPS drift in dense urban areas — fused GPS with a simple dead-reckoning model using last known speed
MQTT message storms during reconnect — added exponential backoff and server-side dedupe
ETA accuracy at peak hours — switched from average speed to time-of-day segmented speeds
mistakes: Used a naive average-speed ETA at first; predictions were off by 10+ minutes in traffic
Ignored power management until devices died mid-route
No simulation environment; every test required a physical bus
learning: Real-time systems need a story for dropped messages and reconnects
Historical data is what makes ETAs believable
A simulator is worth two weeks of field testing
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to design for unreliable networks and to build observability into hardware projects. My biggest leap was in backend real-time architecture.

projects.problemStatement: Students struggle to find peers who have already cleared the courses they are taking, and useful notes and past papers are scattered across messaging apps.
projects.aim: Create a structured peer-learning platform where seniors upload resources and juniors can request help from verified mentors.
objectives: Verify seniority via college email
Support resource uploads with ratings and reviews
Enable real-time chat between mentors and mentees
Keep moderation queue under 24 hours
projects.approach: We built a MERN stack app with Socket.io for chat and S3 for file storage. Verification uses OTP sent to college email domains. A lightweight moderation dashboard lets student moderators approve uploads. We seeded the platform with resources from three departments before launch.
developmentChallenges: File upload reliability on poor connections — added chunked uploads and resumable transfers
Chat scaling during exam weeks — moved from in-memory to Redis adapter for Socket.io
Moderation backlog — added automatic duplicate detection with a hash of file contents
mistakes: Launched chat before moderation, which led to spam within 48 hours
Underestimated storage costs; had to add file size limits and compression
No clear onboarding for mentors; early mentor response rate was very low
learning: Community products need moderation and incentives from day one
Storage and bandwidth costs grow faster than expected
Onboarding is part of the product, not a support task
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned that building a platform is 30% code and 70% community design. I became much better at thinking about incentives, moderation and trust.

projects.problemStatement: Student union elections suffer from low trust, manual counting errors and no verifiable audit trail.
projects.aim: Build a transparent, verifiable voting system where every vote is recorded on-chain and results are auditable by anyone.
objectives: One vote per verified student, enforced on-chain
Voter privacy via zero-knowledge commitments
Public audit trail of all ballots
Handle 2,000 voters without congestion
projects.approach: We wrote a Solidity contract that stores vote commitments and uses a merkle tree for eligibility. Voter identities are verified off-chain by the election committee, and proofs are submitted to the contract. IPFS stores candidate manifestos. We ran a mock election with 300 students in a testnet environment.
developmentChallenges: Gas costs made naive per-vote storage prohibitive — used commitments and batch merkle roots
Wallet UX was a barrier for non-crypto users — built a custodial relayer with signed messages
Testnet congestion caused failed transactions — added retry logic with dynamic gas pricing
mistakes: Started with an on-chain identity registry; gas costs were absurd — pivoted to merkle proofs
Assumed students understood wallets; the first usability test was a disaster
No plan for lost private keys until we added the relayer
learning: Blockchain is an expensive database; use it only where trust requires it
UX is the biggest barrier to Web3 adoption
Design for key loss from the beginning
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to question whether blockchain is actually the right tool. My biggest growth was in cryptographic design and in simplifying complex systems for real users.

projects.problemStatement: Recycling rates stay low because people genuinely do not know which bin an item belongs to, and contamination ruins entire batches.
projects.aim: Build a camera-based assistant that tells users which bin an item belongs in, with local municipal rules.
objectives: Classify 8 waste categories with ≥88% accuracy
Support municipality-specific rule overrides
Run inference offline on mid-range phones
Explain the decision in plain language
projects.approach: We trained an EfficientNet-B0 on a merged dataset and exported to ONNX for React Native inference. A FastAPI service stores municipal rule sets. The app shows the predicted category, confidence and a one-line reason. Field testing is ongoing with a local recycling cooperative.
developmentChallenges: Dataset label noise — two annotators disagreed on 12% of items; added an adjudication step
ONNX runtime size on Android — used a smaller model variant and dynamic loading
Confidence calibration — raw softmax was overconfident; applied temperature scaling
mistakes: Trusted a single public dataset without auditing labels
Skipped calibration until users complained the app was 'too sure'
Did not design for municipal rule updates until late
learning: Dataset auditing is a core engineering task
Calibrated confidence matters more than raw accuracy for user trust
Localisation is a data problem, not just a translation problem
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to treat uncertainty as a first-class product feature. I also got much better at ML evaluation beyond a single accuracy number.

projects.problemStatement: Commercial fitness trackers are expensive and lock users into proprietary clouds, with no way to access raw sensor data.
projects.aim: Build an open, affordable fitness tracker that streams raw sensor data and computes step, heart-rate and sleep metrics locally.
objectives: Track steps with ≥95% accuracy vs. manual count
Measure heart rate within ±5 BPM
Last 5 days on a 200 mAh battery
Expose raw data over BLE and export to CSV
projects.approach: Custom PCB with ESP32, MPU6050 IMU and MAX30102 pulse oximeter. Firmware runs step detection and heart-rate filtering on-device. A Flutter app connects over BLE, syncs to InfluxDB for long-term charts, and exports raw CSVs. We validated against a commercial tracker and manual counts.
developmentChallenges: Motion artefacts corrupted heart-rate readings during exercise — added adaptive filtering and motion gating
BLE throughput limited raw data sync — batched packets and compressed before transfer
Battery life was 2 days initially — reduced sampling rates and added deep sleep between reads
mistakes: Designed the PCB before prototyping on a dev board; one revision was wasted
No calibration flow, so step counts varied by wear position
Underestimated BLE power cost during sync
learning: Prototype on dev boards before committing to a PCB
Signal processing is where wearable accuracy actually comes from
Power budgeting is a firmware concern, not just hardware
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I became comfortable across hardware, firmware and app layers. The biggest lesson was that physical products demand iteration discipline.

projects.problemStatement: During floods and landslides, relief requests, volunteer availability and supply stock are coordinated over scattered phone calls and spreadsheets.
projects.aim: Provide a single coordination platform for relief requests, volunteer matching and supply tracking during disasters.
objectives: Ingest requests via SMS, web and phone
Match volunteers to requests by skill and distance
Track supply inventory across warehouses
Work on intermittent connectivity
projects.approach: Vue 3 front end with Django REST backend, PostGIS for geospatial queries and Celery for async matching and SMS ingestion. The app uses an offline-first service worker and queues requests locally. We ran a tabletop exercise with a local disaster response NGO.
developmentChallenges: SMS ingestion at scale — built a queue with idempotent parsing and deduplication
Offline sync conflicts — implemented last-write-wins with server reconciliation logs
Geospatial matching performance — added spatial indexes and bounding-box pre-filters
mistakes: Assumed reliable connectivity in disaster zones; had to retrofit offline support
No conflict resolution strategy at first, which caused duplicate volunteer assignments
Under-tested SMS parsing with regional dialects and shorthand
learning: Design for the worst network conditions first
Conflict resolution is a product decision, not just a technical one
Real users write SMS very differently from test data
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to design for degraded environments and to treat operations teams as primary users. My growth was as much in empathy as in engineering.

projects.problemStatement: Junior developers rarely get timely, specific code review feedback, and senior reviewers are a bottleneck on every pull request.
projects.aim: Build a GitHub-integrated assistant that reviews pull requests and leaves actionable, line-level comments.
objectives: Comment on security, performance and readability issues
Keep false-positive rate below 15%
Respond within 60 seconds per PR
Support Python and JavaScript initially
projects.approach: We fine-tuned a code LLM on curated review comments and built a GitHub App that posts line-level comments. A FastAPI service orchestrates retrieval, static analysis (Semgrep, ESLint) and LLM review, with Redis caching for repeated diffs. Human reviewers rate each comment to improve the model over time.
developmentChallenges: LLM hallucinations produced confidently wrong comments — grounded prompts with static-analysis findings
Large diffs exceeded context windows — chunked by file and hunk with overlap
Rate limits from GitHub — added per-installation token buckets and queueing
mistakes: Shipped without a feedback loop, so quality plateaued
Tried to review entire repositories instead of diffs; cost and latency exploded
Ignored false positives until users started ignoring all comments
learning: Grounding LLMs with deterministic tools is essential for trust
Feedback loops are what make AI products improve
Precision matters more than recall for developer tooling
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to combine classical static analysis with LLMs rather than treating the model as the whole solution. I also grew a lot in product thinking around trust and precision.

projects.problemStatement: Local digital artists have no trusted marketplace to sell work, and buyers worry about licensing and delivery.
projects.aim: Create a curated marketplace where artists sell licensed digital art with clear usage terms and instant delivery.
objectives: Support multiple licence tiers per artwork
Deliver files instantly and securely after payment
Give artists a transparent earnings dashboard
Keep platform fee under 10%
projects.approach: Next.js front end with Sanity as the CMS, Stripe Connect for artist payouts and Cloudinary for image transformation and delivery. Licence terms are stored as structured data and rendered as a plain-language summary. We onboarded 14 artists before launch.
developmentChallenges: Stripe Connect onboarding complexity for individual artists — built a guided flow with status tracking
Secure file delivery after payment — used signed, short-lived Cloudinary URLs
Search relevance for visual art — added tags, medium and colour filters
mistakes: Underestimated tax and payout complexity across regions
No watermark on preview images initially, leading to free downloads
Curated too strictly at first, which limited supply
learning: Marketplaces are operations-heavy, not just code
Payments and compliance can dominate the roadmap
Supply-side onboarding determines marketplace health
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to think about both sides of a marketplace and to treat legal and payment details as product features. My growth was largely in systems thinking.

projects.problemStatement: Drivers waste 15–20 minutes per trip circling for parking, and lot operators have no live occupancy data.
projects.aim: Detect free parking spots with cameras and expose live availability plus reservations through a web app.
objectives: Detect occupancy with ≥95% accuracy
Update availability within 5 seconds
Support reservations with QR entry
Handle camera outages gracefully
projects.approach: Raspberry Pi cameras run a lightweight OpenCV pipeline that detects vehicles per bay and publishes occupancy over MQTT. A Node.js service maintains live state, and a React app shows a map with reservation and QR entry. We deployed a pilot in one 40-bay lot on campus.
developmentChallenges: Shadows and rain caused false positives — added temporal smoothing and a background model
Camera outages created stale state — added heartbeat monitoring and manual override
Reservation conflicts — implemented optimistic locking with server-side validation
mistakes: Trusted single-frame detection; accuracy was terrible in rain
No fallback when a camera went down, so bays appeared free when occupied
Built reservation UI before defining the conflict rules
learning: Temporal information is essential for reliable vision systems
Every sensor needs a health model and a fallback
Define business rules before building UI
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to treat reliability as a system property and to design fallbacks for every component. My growth was strongest in distributed systems thinking.

projects.problemStatement: Students hesitate to seek mental health support due to stigma and long wait times, and helplines are overwhelmed.
projects.aim: Provide a safe, private chatbot that offers coping strategies, triage and warm hand-off to human counsellors when needed.
objectives: Detect crisis language and escalate immediately
Offer evidence-based coping exercises
Maintain strict privacy with no third-party analytics
Support English and Nepali
projects.approach: We combined Rasa for dialogue flow with a transformer-based crisis classifier. All conversations are encrypted at rest and never used for training without explicit consent. Escalation triggers a warm hand-off to a counsellor queue. A clinical psychologist reviewed all flows and the safety protocol.
developmentChallenges: Crisis detection false negatives — added a high-recall classifier plus keyword fallback
Bilingual NLU quality — collected and annotated native Nepali conversations
Privacy requirements ruled out common analytics — built a self-hosted metrics pipeline
mistakes: Treated the chatbot as a general assistant at first; scope creep hurt safety
Under-invested in Nepali data; early Nepali performance was poor
Did not define escalation ownership until a clinician asked who answers the alert
learning: Safety-critical AI needs explicit failure modes and human ownership
Privacy constraints shape architecture profoundly
Clinical review is non-negotiable for health products
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to design AI responsibly, with safety and privacy as primary constraints. My growth was as much in ethics and process as in engineering.

projects.problemStatement: The existing railway booking flow has a high abandonment rate, poor mobile usability and confusing seat selection.
projects.aim: Redesign the reservation experience with a mobile-first flow, clear seat maps and transparent pricing.
objectives: Cut booking steps from 9 to 5
Achieve WCAG 2.1 AA compliance
Support seat selection with live availability
Reduce booking time by 40% in usability tests
projects.approach: We reverse-engineered the existing flow, ran usability tests with 12 participants and prototyped a new flow in Figma before building in React with TypeScript. Live seat maps are served from a Node.js API backed by Redis for fast availability reads. Playwright covers the critical booking path end-to-end.
developmentChallenges: Live seat availability consistency — used Redis with optimistic locking
Accessibility of the seat map — built a keyboard-navigable grid with ARIA labels
Legacy API quirks — wrote an adapter layer with contract tests
mistakes: Built the UI before finalising the new flow; threw away two weeks of work
Ignored screen-reader testing until late; the seat map needed a full rework
No performance budget, so the first build was slow on 3G
learning: Prototype and test flows before writing UI code
Accessibility must be tested with real assistive tech
Performance budgets keep redesigns honest
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I grew from a UI implementer into a UX-minded engineer. The biggest lesson was that usability testing is cheaper than guessing.

projects.problemStatement: Finding a matching blood donor in an emergency takes hours of phone calls, and donor lists are outdated.
projects.aim: Connect verified donors with recipients in minutes using location and blood-type matching.
objectives: Match donors within 5 km in under 2 minutes
Verify donor eligibility and last donation date
Send push and SMS alerts to matched donors
Maintain a privacy-preserving donor directory
projects.approach: React Native app with Firebase auth and Firestore for donor profiles, plus a Node.js service for matching and Twilio SMS fallback. Donors control visibility and can pause availability. We partnered with a local blood bank for verification and ran a pilot during a donation drive.
developmentChallenges: Matching at scale with geohashing — used geohash prefixes plus distance refinement
SMS deliverability — added retries and a delivery-status dashboard
Privacy vs. reach — implemented radius-based matching without exposing exact locations
mistakes: Stored exact donor addresses initially; had to migrate to coarse locations for privacy
No rate limiting on alerts, so some donors got spammed
Underestimated the need for a web admin for blood bank staff
learning: Privacy must be designed into the data model, not bolted on
Alert fatigue is a real risk in emergency networks
Partners need their own interface, not just an app
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to balance urgency with respect for users' attention and privacy. My growth was strongest in data modelling and partner-facing design.

projects.problemStatement: Farmers and cooperatives plan planting without data-driven yield estimates, leading to oversupply, price crashes and food waste.
projects.aim: Predict crop yield per district using weather, soil and historical production data, and present it in an accessible dashboard.
objectives: Predict yield within 12% MAPE for major crops
Explain the top drivers behind each prediction
Update forecasts monthly with new weather data
Publish an open API for cooperatives
projects.approach: We assembled 15 years of district-level production data, weather records and soil surveys, then trained XGBoost models per crop with time-series cross-validation. SHAP explains feature contributions. A Streamlit dashboard serves forecasts, and a FastAPI endpoint exposes them to cooperatives.
developmentChallenges: Missing and inconsistent historical data — built an imputation and reconciliation pipeline
Leakage from future weather — enforced strict time-based splits
Model drift across districts — added per-district features and periodic retraining
mistakes: Initial model leaked future weather data and looked unrealistically accurate
Ignored district-level heterogeneity; one global model underperformed
Built the dashboard before validating the model with agronomists
learning: Time-series validation is where most data-science projects fail
Explainability builds trust with non-technical stakeholders
Domain experts catch modelling mistakes faster than metrics do
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I became rigorous about validation and about communicating uncertainty. My biggest growth was learning to work with domain experts as equals.

projects.problemStatement: Deaf and hard-of-hearing students face daily communication barriers because few people around them know sign language.
projects.aim: Translate sign language gestures to text and speech in real time using only a webcam.
objectives: Recognise 50 signs with ≥90% accuracy
Run in real time at ≥15 FPS in the browser
Support two-handed signs
Work without specialised hardware
projects.approach: MediaPipe extracts hand landmarks in the browser, and a TensorFlow model classifies sequences of landmarks. Inference runs client-side via TensorFlow.js, with a FastAPI fallback for heavier models. We are collecting a custom dataset with deaf participants to ensure signer diversity.
developmentChallenges: Signer-dependent overfitting — added signer-independent splits and augmentation
Temporal segmentation of continuous signing — added a sliding window with a neutral-pose trigger
Browser performance on low-end laptops — reduced landmark resolution and model size
mistakes: Trained on a single signer initially; accuracy collapsed for new users
Ignored temporal boundaries, treating each frame independently
Did not involve deaf users until the third month
learning: Signer diversity is essential in sign-language ML
Temporal modelling is unavoidable for real signing
Co-design with the community is a technical advantage
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to build ML with, not for, the community it serves. My growth was strongest in data collection ethics and temporal modelling.

projects.problemStatement: Small neighbourhood shops lose customers to large delivery apps that charge high commissions and ignore small vendors.
projects.aim: Build a hyperlocal delivery platform owned by neighbourhood shopkeepers with fair commissions and local rider pools.
objectives: Onboard shops in under 10 minutes
Route riders with batched pickups
Keep commission under 8%
Support cash and digital payment
projects.approach: SvelteKit storefront with Node.js backend, PostgreSQL for orders and Redis for live rider state. Routing uses a greedy batching algorithm over MapLibre. Shops get a QR-based onboarding flow; riders get a lightweight PWA. We piloted with 12 shops and 6 riders in one neighbourhood.
developmentChallenges: Rider batching without overcomplicating — chose a simple greedy algorithm with clear rules
Cash reconciliation — built a daily settlement report and rider float tracking
Shop onboarding friction — replaced form-heavy signup with a guided QR flow
mistakes: Tried to build a full routing optimiser; wasted three weeks before simplifying
Ignored cash handling workflows until pilot week
Over-engineered the rider app; riders wanted speed, not features
learning: Simple algorithms with clear rules beat complex ones in operations
Cash is still king in many local economies
Riders are the primary users; design for one-handed use
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to resist over-engineering and to design for real operational constraints. My growth was strongest in product simplification.

projects.problemStatement: Students in smaller cities lack access to career counsellors and rely on incomplete advice from peers and social media.
projects.aim: Provide structured career guidance, aptitude assessments and mentor connections to students regardless of location.
objectives: Deliver a validated aptitude assessment
Recommend 5 career paths with reasoning
Connect students with vetted mentors
Support low-bandwidth usage
projects.approach: Next.js front end with Supabase for auth and data, and an LLM layer that turns assessment results into personalised career explanations grounded in a curated career database. Mentor matching is rule-based over interests and location. We tested with 80 students across three schools.
developmentChallenges: LLM output consistency — grounded prompts with a structured career schema and output validation
Low-bandwidth performance — optimised images and used server components to cut JS
Mentor supply — built a lightweight mentor onboarding and availability calendar
mistakes: Let the LLM invent career paths; had to constrain it to a curated database
Over-invested in a fancy UI before validating the assessment
No plan for mentor no-shows until students complained
learning: LLMs are best used to explain, not to invent facts
Assessment validity matters more than UI polish
Marketplaces need reliability guarantees on the supply side
projects.summaryOfGrowth: I learned to use AI as an explanation layer over curated data. My growth was strongest in responsible AI use and in validation-driven design.
